subject: Introduction to Forensic Nursing and Indian Laws
unit_title: Forensic Science and Violence
question: Define forensic science. Explain its history and importance in medical science.
answer_html:
Definition

  • The word forensic comes from the Latin forensis, meaning "of or before the forum" – the public place where legal matters were discussed in ancient Rome.
  • Forensic science is the application of scientific knowledge and methods to matters of law – to the investigation of crimes and civil disputes and to the presentation of evidence in courts of law.
  • It helps to answer questions such as what happened, how, when, where and by whom.

History

  • Ancient period – Kautilya's Arthashastra (India, about the 4th century BCE) described examination of the bodies of persons who died suddenly to determine whether death was due to poisoning, hanging or injury. In ancient China, the book Xi Yuan Ji Lu (The Washing Away of Wrongs, 13th century) by Song Ci was an early manual of forensic medicine.
  • 16th–18th centuries – development of autopsy and legal medicine in Europe (Ambroise Paré; Paolo Zacchia, often called the father of legal medicine).
  • 19th century
    • Mathieu Orfila – father of toxicology (1813).
    • Alphonse Bertillon – anthropometry (body measurements) for identifying criminals.
    • Fingerprinting – Sir William Herschel in Bengal, Henry Faulds and Francis Galton; the Henry classification system developed by Edward Henry with Indian officers Azizul Haque and Hem Chandra Bose; the world's first fingerprint bureau was established in Kolkata in 1897.
  • Early 20th century – Edmond Locard established a police laboratory in Lyon and formulated Locard's exchange principle ("every contact leaves a trace"); Karl Landsteiner's discovery of ABO blood groups (1901) enabled blood-group typing in investigations.
  • Late 20th century – DNA profiling (fingerprinting) developed by Sir Alec Jeffreys (1984–85) revolutionised identification.
  • Modern period – digital and cyber forensics, forensic genomics, advanced toxicology and imaging (virtual autopsy); in India, Central and State Forensic Science Laboratories, the National Forensic Sciences University and the forensic investigation requirements of the new criminal laws (2023).

Branches of forensic science

  • Forensic medicine (medical jurisprudence) and forensic pathology (autopsy, cause of death).
  • Forensic toxicology (poisons, drugs, alcohol).
  • Forensic serology and DNA analysis (blood, semen, saliva).
  • Forensic odontology (teeth and bite marks), forensic anthropology (skeletal remains).
  • Forensic entomology (insects to estimate time since death).
  • Forensic psychiatry and psychology.
  • Fingerprint science, questioned documents, ballistics, chemistry, physics, and digital/cyber forensics.
  • Forensic nursing – application of nursing science to forensic cases.

Importance in medical science and health care

  1. Determination of the cause, manner and time of death through medico-legal autopsy.
  2. Identification of the living and the dead – in disasters, unknown bodies, missing persons (DNA, teeth, fingerprints).
  3. Examination and care of victims of assault, sexual violence, child abuse, domestic violence and elder abuse – with collection of evidence and documentation.
  4. Detection of poisoning and drug overdose, and guidance on treatment.
  5. Estimation of age (for juvenile justice, marriage, employment).
  6. Determination of paternity and maternity (DNA).
  7. Assessment of injuries – nature, weapon, duration, severity (simple or grievous hurt).
  8. Investigation of medical negligence cases and providing expert opinion.
  9. Medico-legal duties of health professionals – reporting medico-legal cases, preserving evidence, certification and testifying in court.
  10. Public health and prevention – data on violence, injuries, suicides, poisonings and deaths help in prevention programmes and policy.
  11. Protection of human rights – documentation of custodial violence and torture.

Relevance to nurses – nurses are often the first health professionals to see victims in emergency departments, wards and the community; knowledge of forensic science helps them recognise forensic cases, preserve evidence, document accurately and support justice for patients.

Scope of forensic science in India today – forensic evidence is becoming central to criminal justice. The new criminal laws (2023) make forensic investigation at the crime scene compulsory for serious offences, encourage video recording and electronic evidence, and give importance to timely medical examination of victims. This increases the demand for trained forensic experts, including forensic nurses in hospitals, sexual assault care centres, emergency departments and correctional settings.

Medico-legal cases commonly seen in hospitals – road traffic accidents, assaults and injuries, burns, poisoning, suspected homicide or suicide, sexual offences, unnatural deaths, deaths in custody or soon after surgery, and cases brought dead – all of which require forensic knowledge for correct management.

Conclusion Forensic science is the application of science to law. It developed from ancient texts like the Arthashastra through toxicology, fingerprinting (with the first fingerprint bureau in Kolkata), Locard's exchange principle and DNA profiling to modern digital forensics. It is important in medical science for determining cause of death, identification, care of victims, detection of poisoning, age estimation, injury assessment, negligence cases, medico-legal duties and prevention of violence, and nurses play a key role in it.

subject: Introduction to Forensic Nursing and Indian Laws

question: Define violence. Explain its types, epidemiology and the sources of data on violence.
answer_html:
Definition Violence is "the intentional use of physical force or power, threatened or actual, against oneself, another person, or against a group or community, that either results in or has a high likelihood of resulting in injury, death, psychological harm, maldevelopment or deprivation" (World Health Organization, World Report on Violence and Health, 2002).

Types of violence (WHO typology) A. By who commits it

  1. Self-directed violence – suicidal behaviour and self-harm.
  2. Interpersonal violence
    • Family and intimate partner violence – domestic violence, child abuse and neglect, elder abuse, dowry-related violence.
    • Community violence – among unrelated persons (youth violence, assault by strangers, sexual violence by acquaintances or strangers, violence in workplaces, schools, prisons and institutions).
  3. Collective violence – by groups for social, political or economic aims (riots, terrorism, war, communal violence). B. By the nature of the act
  • Physical – hitting, kicking, burning, strangulation, use of weapons.
  • Sexual – rape, sexual assault, molestation, sexual harassment, trafficking.
  • Psychological (emotional) – threats, humiliation, intimidation, isolation, controlling behaviour.
  • Deprivation or neglect – withholding food, care, medical treatment, education or money (economic abuse).

Epidemiology

  • Global – violence is a leading cause of death and disability, especially among young people. WHO estimates that about one in three women worldwide has experienced physical or sexual violence by an intimate partner or sexual violence by a non-partner in her lifetime. Large numbers of children experience physical punishment and abuse, and suicide claims hundreds of thousands of lives each year.
  • India
    • The National Family Health Survey-5 (2019–21) found that about 29% of ever-married women aged 18–49 had ever experienced physical or sexual violence by their husbands; many never sought help.
    • National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) data show several lakh cases of crimes against women every year – mainly cruelty by husband or relatives, assault on women with intent to outrage modesty, kidnapping and rape – and large numbers of crimes against children, especially under the POCSO Act.
    • A national study by the Ministry of Women and Child Development (2007) reported that more than half of children surveyed had faced some form of sexual abuse.
    • Elder abuse, workplace violence (including violence against health workers) and road rage are also important.

Risk factors (ecological model)

  • Individual – young age, alcohol and drug use, history of abuse in childhood, mental illness, low education.
  • Relationship – family conflict, controlling partners, dowry demands, poor parenting.
  • Community – poverty, unemployment, overcrowding, availability of weapons and drugs, weak policing.
  • Society – gender inequality, patriarchal norms that accept violence, social acceptance of corporal punishment, conflicts.

Consequences – injuries, disability and death; unwanted pregnancy, unsafe abortion, STIs and HIV; depression, PTSD, substance use and suicide; poor child development; economic loss; intergenerational cycle of violence.

Sources of data on violence

  1. National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) – publishes "Crime in India", "Accidental Deaths and Suicides in India (ADSI)" and "Prison Statistics India", based on police records (FIRs).
  2. National Family Health Survey (NFHS) – the domestic violence module provides population-based data on spousal violence and help-seeking.
  3. Hospital records – emergency registers, medico-legal case (MLC) registers, post-mortem records, injury surveillance.
  4. Police records – FIRs, case diaries and investigations.
  5. Helpline and support services data – Women Helpline 181, Childline 1098, One Stop Centres, Emergency Response Support System 112.
  6. Special surveys and research studies – national and state surveys on child abuse, elder abuse, workplace violence.
  7. Court records, records of child welfare committees, NCPCR and human rights commissions.
  8. International sources – WHO and UN reports and the Global Burden of Disease study.

Limitations of data – violence is greatly under-reported because of stigma, fear, dependence on the abuser, lack of awareness and distrust of police; police data reflect only reported cases, and surveys depend on respondents' willingness to disclose.

Role of the nurse – recognising and documenting violence carefully in hospital records improves the quality of data and helps victims receive care and justice.

Conclusion Violence, as defined by WHO, is the intentional use of force or power that causes or is likely to cause harm; it may be self-directed, interpersonal (family/intimate partner and community) or collective, and physical, sexual, psychological or neglectful in nature. It is common globally and in India – about 29% of ever-married women report spousal violence (NFHS-5) – and is driven by individual, relationship, community and societal factors. Data come from NCRB, NFHS, hospital and MLC records, police records, helplines, surveys and courts, though under-reporting is a major limitation.

question: Explain sexual abuse of children and women – types, indicators, consequences and the role of the nurse in medico-legal care.
answer_html:
Introduction Sexual abuse is any sexual act or attempt to obtain a sexual act, unwanted sexual comments or advances, or acts directed against a person's sexuality using coercion, by any person regardless of relationship, in any setting. Children cannot give consent; therefore any sexual activity with a child (below 18 years) is abuse. Sexual violence is a grave violation of human rights with lifelong physical and psychological consequences.

Types

  1. Rape and penetrative sexual assault – including by husbands of minor wives, acquaintances, relatives (incest) and strangers; gang rape.
  2. Non-penetrative sexual assault – touching, fondling, molestation.
  3. Sexual harassment – unwelcome comments, gestures, showing pornography, stalking, online harassment.
  4. Child sexual abuse – by family members, neighbours, teachers or caregivers, often with grooming (building trust and secrecy); online exploitation and child pornography.
  5. Sexual exploitation and trafficking – commercial sexual exploitation, forced prostitution.
  6. Sexual violence in conflicts and institutions (custodial, hostels, workplaces).

Indicators (warning signs)

  • Physical (in children)
    • Pain, itching, bleeding, bruises or injuries in the genital or anal area.
    • Torn or stained underclothes; difficulty in walking or sitting.
    • STIs or pregnancy in a child or young adolescent; recurrent urinary infections.
  • Behavioural (in children)
    • Sudden fear of a particular person or place; withdrawal, depression, anxiety, nightmares.
    • Bed-wetting, sexual behaviour or knowledge inappropriate for age.
    • Decline in school performance, running away, self-harm, substance use.
  • In women
    • Unexplained injuries, especially to the breasts, thighs, genitals and face.
    • Repeated visits with vague complaints; anxiety, depression, suicidal attempts.
    • A controlling partner who will not leave her alone.

Consequences

  • Physical – genital and other injuries, STIs including HIV, unwanted pregnancy, unsafe abortion, chronic pelvic pain.
  • Psychological – fear, shame, guilt, post-traumatic stress disorder, depression, anxiety, sleep and eating problems, suicidal behaviour, substance use.
  • Social – stigma, rejection by family, school drop-out, loss of employment, difficulties in relationships; for children, impaired development and later revictimisation.

Medico-legal care – role of the nurse The MoHFW Guidelines and Protocols for Medico-legal Care for Survivors/Victims of Sexual Violence (2014) emphasise survivor-centred, comprehensive and gender-sensitive care. The nurse's role:

  1. Immediate care and privacy
    • Receive the survivor in a private area; ensure safety; give priority treatment of life-threatening injuries.
    • Under Section 397 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), every hospital, public or private, must give free first aid and medical treatment immediately to victims of rape, acid attack and sexual offences against children, and inform the police.
    • Treatment does not depend on an FIR or police requisition.
  2. Informed consent
    • Explain each step and obtain written informed consent for examination, evidence collection and treatment (from the survivor if 12 years or older, or from a parent or guardian for younger children).
    • Respect the right to refuse any part.
    • Under BNSS Section 184, a rape survivor is examined by a registered medical practitioner with her consent, as soon as possible.
  3. Assist in history and examination
    • Be present as a female attendant; support the survivor emotionally.
    • Help document the history in the survivor's words, the time since the assault and the acts involved.
    • The "two-finger test" must not be done – it has been prohibited by the Supreme Court; no comment is made on past sexual experience.
  4. Evidence collection (as per protocol, with consent)
    • Clothing in paper bags.
    • Swabs from the body and genital areas; nail scrapings and debris; hair combings.
    • Blood and urine for toxicology (in drug-facilitated assault).
    • Each item is labelled, dried, sealed and handed over to the police with documentation of the chain of custody.
  5. Treatment
    • Emergency contraception (within 72–120 hours); pregnancy testing.
    • Prophylaxis for STIs; HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (within 72 hours); hepatitis B and tetanus vaccination.
    • Treatment of injuries.
  6. Psychosocial support
    • Psychological first aid – listen, believe, do not blame.
    • Assess suicide risk; provide counselling and referral to mental health services and One Stop Centres.
  7. Reporting and legal duties
    • Child sexual abuse must be reported to the Special Juvenile Police Unit or local police under Section 19 of the POCSO Act; failure to report is punishable.
    • For adults, police are informed as required by law, while respecting the survivor's choice regarding a police complaint.
    • The identity of a survivor must never be disclosed (BNS Section 72).
  8. Documentation – accurate, objective, legible notes using the survivor's own words, body diagrams, time and date; confidential storage.
  9. Follow-up – review for test results, completion of PEP, vaccination, pregnancy and mental health.
  10. Prevention and education – teach children about body safety ("good touch–bad touch"), educate parents, support community awareness and safe environments.

Conclusion Sexual abuse of children and women takes many forms – rape, assault, harassment, incest, exploitation and trafficking – and shows physical and behavioural indicators with serious physical, psychological and social consequences. The nurse provides survivor-centred medico-legal care: free immediate treatment (BNSS 397), privacy, informed consent, support during examination without the two-finger test, careful evidence collection and chain of custody, emergency contraception, STI and HIV prophylaxis, psychosocial support, mandatory reporting of child abuse under POCSO, confidentiality, documentation and follow-up.

question: Explain the forensic science laboratory – its organisation and functions.
answer_html:
Introduction A forensic science laboratory (FSL) is a scientific laboratory that examines physical and biological evidence sent by the police, courts and hospitals and gives expert reports and opinions to help in investigation and trial.

Organisation in India

  • Central Forensic Science Laboratories (CFSLs) under the Directorate of Forensic Science Services (Ministry of Home Affairs), located in cities such as Chandigarh, Kolkata, Hyderabad, New Delhi, Pune, Bhopal and Guwahati; the Central Bureau of Investigation also has its own CFSL.
  • State Forensic Science Laboratories in each state, with Regional FSLs in divisions/districts.
  • Mobile forensic units (vans) that reach crime scenes – increasingly important because the BNSS, 2023 requires forensic experts to visit crime scenes for offences punishable with seven years or more.
  • Fingerprint bureaux, questioned-document examiners and cyber forensic laboratories.
  • Education and research – the National Forensic Sciences University and forensic science departments.

Divisions and their work

  1. Biology and serology – blood, semen, saliva, hair, fibres, species identification.
  2. DNA profiling – identification of victims and offenders, paternity disputes, disaster victims.
  3. Toxicology – poisons, drugs and alcohol in viscera, blood, urine and vomitus.
  4. Chemistry – narcotics, explosives, acids (acid attacks), petroleum products, adulterants.
  5. Physics – glass, paint, soil, tool marks, fire and traffic accident analysis.
  6. Ballistics – firearms, bullets, cartridges, gunshot residue.
  7. Questioned documents – handwriting, signatures, forgery.
  8. Fingerprints and footprints.
  9. Cyber and digital forensics – mobile phones, computers, CCTV and audio-video analysis.
  10. Photography and scene documentation; lie detection/psychology units in some laboratories.

Functions

  • Scientific examination and analysis of evidence.
  • Expert reports and opinions; scientists appear as expert witnesses in court.
  • Crime-scene assistance and reconstruction.
  • Training of police, doctors and nurses in evidence handling.
  • Research and development of new methods; maintenance of databases.

Relevance to nurses – samples from hospitals (viscera, blood, swabs, clothing) reach the FSL; the nurse must collect, label, seal, store and hand over samples correctly with forms and chain of custody, because contaminated or poorly documented samples may be rejected and justice denied.

Conclusion Forensic science laboratories – central, state, regional and mobile units – examine biological, chemical, physical and digital evidence in divisions such as serology, DNA, toxicology, chemistry, physics, ballistics, documents, fingerprints and cyber forensics, and provide expert reports, crime-scene support and training; correct sample handling by nurses is vital for their work.

question: What is Locard's exchange principle?
answer_html:
Locard's exchange principle was stated by the French criminologist Dr Edmond Locard (1877–1966), a pioneer of forensic science.

  • It states that "every contact leaves a trace" – whenever two objects or persons come into contact, there is a transfer of material between them.
  • For example, an offender may leave fingerprints, hair, blood, semen, skin cells or fibres on the victim or at the scene, and carry away traces (soil, fibres, blood) from them. Importance – it is the basis of trace evidence collection; nurses must handle victims' clothing and bodies carefully, wear gloves, avoid contamination and preserve such traces.

question: What is the National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB)? Name its publications.
tags: Accidental Deaths and Suicides in India
answer_html:
The National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) is an agency under the Ministry of Home Affairs, set up in 1986, that collects, compiles and analyses crime data reported by the police of all states and union territories and maintains national crime databases. Main publications (annual)

  • Crime in India – crimes against women, children, the elderly and others.
  • Accidental Deaths and Suicides in India (ADSI).
  • Prison Statistics India. Use – these reports are major sources of data on violence for planning prevention and policy; however, they include only cases reported to the police.

question: Define forensic nursing. Explain its history, scope and the roles and responsibilities of the forensic nurse.

diagram.caption: Scope of forensic nursing
labels: the forensic nurse at the centre linking clinical care with the legal system
with subspecialties around – sexual assault nurse examiner
forensic gerontology and paediatric forensic nursing

answer_html:
Definition

  • Forensic nursing is the application of nursing science to public or legal proceedings – the care of patients (victims and perpetrators) affected by violence, trauma and crime, combined with the collection of evidence, documentation and testimony to help the legal system.
  • The International Association of Forensic Nurses (IAFN) describes it as the practice of nursing globally when health and legal systems intersect.
  • The forensic nurse thus has a dual responsibility – to provide holistic care and to preserve the rights and evidence needed for justice.

History and development

  • Nurses have always cared for victims of violence and injury, but forensic nursing as a specialty began in the 1980s in the USA and Canada.
  • Virginia Lynch, regarded as the founder of forensic nursing, developed the concept and its first educational programmes.
  • Sexual Assault Nurse Examiner (SANE) programmes started in the late 1970s and 1980s to give survivors specialised, timely care.
  • The International Association of Forensic Nurses was founded in 1992, and the American Nurses Association recognised forensic nursing as a specialty in 1995; certification programmes followed.
  • In India, forensic nursing is a newer field. The Indian Nursing Council introduced the course "Introduction to Forensic Nursing and Indian Laws" in the B.Sc Nursing curriculum (2021), and specialised training is being developed. The rising number of medico-legal cases, sexual offences and new criminal laws requiring forensic evidence increase its importance.

Scope of forensic nursing A. Practice settings

  • Hospital emergency and trauma departments, ICUs and wards (medico-legal cases).
  • Sexual assault care centres and One Stop Centres.
  • Paediatric units – child abuse and neglect.
  • Psychiatric forensic units – mentally ill offenders.
  • Correctional facilities – prisons and juvenile homes.
  • Medical examiner and coroner offices, mortuaries – death investigation.
  • Community – domestic violence, elder abuse, home visits, schools.
  • Disaster and mass-casualty settings – identification of victims, evidence.
  • Legal firms, insurance companies and courts – as consultants. B. Areas of practice and subspecialties
  1. Sexual assault nurse examiner (SANE) – care of sexual violence survivors.
  2. Forensic emergency and trauma nursing – assault, gunshot, stab, burn and road accident victims.
  3. Forensic psychiatric nursing – assessment and care of mentally ill offenders; risk assessment.
  4. Correctional (custody) nursing – health care of prisoners and detainees.
  5. Nurse death investigator – scene investigation and assisting in determining the cause and manner of death.
  6. Forensic paediatric nursing – child abuse and neglect.
  7. Forensic gerontology nursing – elder abuse and neglect.
  8. Legal nurse consultant – analysing medical records and advising lawyers in health-related cases.
  9. Forensic nurse educator and researcher.
  10. Clinical forensic nurse specialist – in intimate partner violence, human trafficking, organ donation and transplant issues.

Roles and responsibilities of the forensic nurse

  1. Holistic care – physical, psychological, social, cultural and spiritual care of victims, families and sometimes perpetrators, with dignity and non-judgemental attitudes.
  2. Assessment and identification of forensic cases – recognising signs of abuse, assault, neglect, poisoning and suspicious injuries.
  3. Evidence management – recognition, collection, preservation and documentation of evidence; maintenance of the chain of custody.
  4. Documentation – accurate, objective, detailed records; injury descriptions, body diagrams, photographs (with consent).
  5. Reporting – medico-legal intimation to police; mandatory reporting of child sexual abuse (POCSO) and other legally required reports.
  6. Crisis intervention and counselling; referral to support services (One Stop Centres, legal aid, shelters, mental health services).
  7. Advocacy – protecting patients' rights, privacy and confidentiality; ensuring free treatment as required by law.
  8. Collaboration with the forensic team – doctors, forensic pathologists, police, forensic scientists, social workers and lawyers.
  9. Testimony – appearing in court as a witness of fact or, when qualified, an expert witness.
  10. Education and prevention – teaching staff and the community about violence prevention and evidence preservation; research on violence.
  11. Death investigation – care of the body, preservation of evidence, support to families.

Conclusion Forensic nursing applies nursing science to legal proceedings, combining care of patients affected by violence and trauma with evidence collection, documentation and testimony. Started in the 1980s by Virginia Lynch and recognised internationally since the 1990s, it is now part of the Indian B.Sc Nursing curriculum. Its scope covers hospitals, sexual assault centres, prisons, psychiatric units, death investigation, the community and disasters, with subspecialties such as SANE, forensic psychiatric, correctional, paediatric and gerontological nursing, nurse death investigation and legal nurse consultancy. The forensic nurse provides holistic care, identifies cases, manages evidence, documents, reports, counsels, advocates, collaborates, testifies and educates.

subject: Introduction to Forensic Nursing and Indian Laws
unit_title: Forensic Nursing
question: Explain the ethical issues in forensic nursing.
answer_html:
Introduction Forensic nurses work where health care and the legal system meet, which creates special ethical challenges. They must balance the patient's welfare and rights with legal duties and the needs of justice.

Ethical issues

  1. Dual role – caregiver and evidence collector
    • The primary duty is patient care; evidence collection must never delay life-saving treatment or harm the patient.
    • The nurse must avoid acting as an investigator against the patient's interests.
  2. Informed consent
    • Examination, photographs and evidence collection require voluntary informed consent; survivors may refuse some or all steps.
    • Issues arise with unconscious patients, intoxicated persons, children, persons with mental illness and accused persons examined at police request (where the law may permit examination without consent).
  3. Confidentiality versus legal reporting
    • Patients' information is confidential, but the law requires reporting of medico-legal cases and mandatory reporting of child sexual abuse (POCSO).
    • The nurse discloses only what is required, to the proper authority, and protects the identity of sexual offence survivors.
  4. Privacy and dignity – during examination, photography and handling of the body; limiting persons present.
  5. Objectivity and avoidance of bias – documentation must be factual, unbiased and truthful, without personal opinions or assumptions about guilt; non-judgemental care for both victims and accused.
  6. Rights of prisoners and accused persons – equal quality of care, protection from torture or ill-treatment; ethical concerns about restraint, handcuffing during treatment, or being asked to participate in punishment.
  7. Justice and equity – free and prompt treatment for all victims regardless of status, caste, gender or ability to pay.
  8. Cultural and gender sensitivity – respecting beliefs, offering same-gender examiners when possible.
  9. Truthfulness in testimony – giving honest evidence in court within one's competence.
  10. Professional boundaries – avoiding personal involvement with victims or offenders; avoiding conflicts of interest.
  11. Vicarious trauma and self-care – repeated exposure to violence can cause emotional distress; ethical practice includes supervision and support for the nurse.
  12. Media and social media – never disclosing details of cases or survivors.

Ethical principles applied – respect for autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice, veracity, fidelity and confidentiality, guided by the nursing code of ethics and the law.

Conclusion Ethical issues in forensic nursing include the dual role of caregiver and evidence collector, informed consent and refusal, confidentiality versus mandatory reporting, privacy and dignity, objectivity, prisoners' rights, justice, cultural sensitivity, truthful testimony, boundaries, vicarious trauma and media disclosure; forensic nurses resolve them by putting patient welfare first while fulfilling legal duties honestly.

subject: Introduction to Forensic Nursing and Indian Laws

question: Explain the Indian Nursing Council Act and the State Nursing Council Acts, with reference to the National Nursing and Midwifery Commission Act, 2023.
tags: National Nursing and Midwifery Commission Act 2023
importance for forensic and legal practice
answer_html:
1. Indian Nursing Council (INC) Act, 1947

  • Passed by Parliament in 1947 to constitute the Indian Nursing Council as a statutory body to establish a uniform standard of training for nurses, midwives, ANMs and health visitors (amended in 1950 and later).
  • Constitution – a president, vice-president and members (ex-officio, elected and nominated) representing government, nursing services, education and state councils.
  • Main functions
    • Prescribing minimum standards of education – syllabus, curriculum, admission criteria, duration, faculty and infrastructure.
    • Recognition of nursing qualifications included in the schedules of the Act; withdrawal of recognition from institutions not meeting standards.
    • Inspection of institutions and examinations.
    • Maintaining the Indian Nurses Register (now through the Nurses Registration and Tracking System) and advising on reciprocity with foreign qualifications.
    • Promoting continuing education and research.

2. State Nursing Council Acts

  • Each state has its own Act (e.g. the Maharashtra Nurses Act constituting the Maharashtra Nursing Council).
  • Main functions
    • Registration of nurses and midwives who qualify from recognised institutions – registration is necessary to practise legally in the state; renewal of registration as per state rules.
    • Maintaining the state register.
    • Conducting examinations and inspections (in some states).
    • Disciplinary powers – inquiry into complaints of professional misconduct, negligence or criminal conviction; removal or suspension of a name from the register after due process.
    • Prescribing the code of conduct and continuing nursing education requirements.
    • Offences – practising without registration or misusing the title of registered nurse are punishable.

3. National Nursing and Midwifery Commission (NNMC) Act, 2023

  • Passed by Parliament in August 2023 to replace the INC Act, 1947 with a National Nursing and Midwifery Commission, supported by autonomous boards for education, assessment and rating, and ethics and registration, and by State Nursing and Midwifery Commissions.
  • It provides for a National Register of nurses and midwives, regulation of nursing and midwifery education and services, assessment of institutions, and standards of professional conduct and ethics.
  • The repeal of the INC Act takes effect from a date notified by the Central Government; until the Commission is constituted, the Indian Nursing Council continues to function.

Importance for forensic and legal practice

  • Only registered nurses can legally practise; registration status is relevant in negligence cases and when a nurse gives evidence.
  • Nursing councils define the scope of practice and standards of conduct; acting beyond scope or unethically may lead to disciplinary action and legal liability.
  • Councils protect the public by removing those guilty of misconduct.
  • The INC curriculum includes forensic nursing, developing nurses' medico-legal competence.

Conclusion The INC Act, 1947 established the Indian Nursing Council to set uniform standards of nursing education and recognise qualifications, while State Nursing Council Acts provide for registration, renewal, registers and disciplinary control over nurses. The NNMC Act, 2023 provides for a National Nursing and Midwifery Commission to replace the INC, which continues to function until the Commission is constituted. These laws define who may practise and the standards nurses must meet – important in all medico-legal and forensic situations.

subject: Introduction to Forensic Nursing and Indian Laws
unit_title: Forensic Nursing
question: Who is a sexual assault nurse examiner (SANE)?
answer_html:
A sexual assault nurse examiner (SANE) is a registered nurse with specialised education and clinical training in the medical-forensic care of survivors of sexual assault. Functions

  • Provides survivor-centred, trauma-informed care – emotional support, privacy, informed consent.
  • Takes the history and performs a head-to-toe and genital examination, documenting injuries.
  • Collects and preserves forensic evidence using sexual assault evidence kits, maintaining the chain of custody.
  • Gives emergency contraception, STI prophylaxis and HIV PEP; refers for counselling and support services.
  • Testifies in court as a fact or expert witness. SANE programmes improve the quality of evidence, reduce waiting times and reduce re-traumatisation of survivors.

subject: Introduction to Forensic Nursing and Indian Laws
unit_title: Forensic Nursing
question: What is a legal nurse consultant?
answer_html:
A legal nurse consultant is an experienced registered nurse who uses nursing and health-care knowledge to advise lawyers, courts, insurance companies and health-care organisations on health-related legal matters. Functions

  • Reviewing and analysing medical records and preparing chronologies of care.
  • Identifying whether the standard of care was met in negligence and malpractice cases.
  • Interpreting medical terminology, injuries and treatment for legal teams.
  • Locating and preparing expert witnesses; sometimes testifying.
  • Assisting in personal injury, workers' compensation, insurance and criminal cases, and in risk management in hospitals.

question: List the members of the forensic team and explain their roles. Add a note on how the nurse assists the forensic team in care beyond the nurse's scope.

diagram.caption: The multidisciplinary forensic team
labels: victim and family at the centre
linked to the forensic nurse and treating doctors (care)
forensic medicine expert and pathologist (medico-legal examination and autopsy)

answer_html:
Introduction Forensic cases need the combined work of health, legal and social professionals. The forensic team is a multidisciplinary group that provides care to victims, investigates the case scientifically and helps the court reach a just decision.

Members and their roles

  1. Forensic nurse
    • Provides holistic care to victims (and accused persons when in health care).
    • Identifies forensic cases, collects and preserves evidence, documents injuries and history.
    • Maintains the chain of custody; informs police as required.
    • Supports the family; coordinates with other team members; may testify in court.
  2. Emergency physician / treating doctor / medical officer
    • Resuscitation and treatment; medico-legal examination and certification of injuries.
    • Writes the medico-legal case (MLC) report; issues wound certificates; refers to specialists.
  3. Forensic medicine specialist (medico-legal expert)
    • Clinical forensic examinations – sexual offences, age estimation, injury assessment, examination of the accused.
    • Gives expert opinion and testimony.
  4. Forensic pathologist
    • Performs the medico-legal autopsy to determine cause, manner and time of death; identifies the deceased.
    • Collects viscera and other samples for analysis.
  5. Police / investigating officer (IO)
    • Registers the FIR, investigates the crime, records statements.
    • Conducts the inquest in unnatural deaths; requests medical examination and post-mortem.
    • Seizes and forwards evidence to the forensic laboratory; files the charge sheet.
  6. Crime-scene investigators and forensic photographers/videographers – document and protect the scene, collect physical evidence (fingerprints, weapons, blood stains, digital devices); under the BNSS, forensic experts visit scenes of serious offences.
  7. Forensic scientists (forensic science laboratory)
    • DNA analysts and serologists, toxicologists, chemists, ballistics experts and document examiners.
    • Cyber forensic experts, fingerprint experts.
    • They analyse samples and give expert reports.
  8. Other forensic specialists
    • Forensic odontologist – teeth and bite marks.
    • Forensic anthropologist – skeletal remains.
    • Forensic entomologist – insects and time since death.
    • Radiologist – fractures, foreign bodies, age estimation.
  9. Forensic psychiatrist and psychologist – assess mental state of victims and accused (fitness to stand trial, insanity defence); treat trauma.
  10. Medical social worker and counsellors – crisis intervention, emotional support, rehabilitation, links with shelters, One Stop Centres, legal aid and compensation schemes.
  11. Child protection officials – Child Welfare Committee, Special Juvenile Police Unit, District Child Protection Unit, support persons (in POCSO cases).
  12. Legal professionals
    • Public prosecutor presents the case for the State.
    • Defence lawyer represents the accused.
    • Magistrates and judges record statements (including dying declarations), conduct magistrate inquests, try cases and deliver judgment.
  13. Hospital administration and medical records staff – maintain MLC registers and records, provide copies to authorities as per law.

Principles of teamwork – a shared goal of patient welfare and justice, clear roles, timely communication, respect for each discipline, confidentiality, standardised protocols, and avoiding duplication that could re-traumatise the victim (e.g. one comprehensive examination).

Assisting the forensic team in care beyond the nurse's scope Some procedures are performed by doctors or specialists, but the nurse assists by:

  • Preparing the patient – explaining procedures, obtaining or witnessing consent, providing privacy and a female attendant.
  • Preparing equipment – sexual assault evidence kits, swabs, containers, labels, envelopes, preservatives, camera, body diagrams.
  • Assisting during examination – positioning, handing swabs, labelling specimens immediately, recording findings dictated by the doctor.
  • Assisting in procedures – suturing, X-rays, operative care, gastric lavage (preserving the first sample of gastric contents in poisoning cases).
  • Assisting the pathologist in hospital-based autopsies or preparing the body for transfer to the mortuary without disturbing evidence.
  • Arranging consultations – psychiatrist, paediatrician, gynaecologist, counsellor, social worker.
  • Supporting the police and magistrate – informing them when the patient is fit to give a statement; arranging recording of a dying declaration if the patient's condition is critical, and remaining present as a witness if required.
  • Never exceeding her competence – the nurse does not give opinions on the cause of injuries or alter documentation, but records observations accurately and reports.

Example of team working – a 14-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department after sexual assault. The nurse provides privacy and comfort, informs the medical officer, and the case is registered as an MLC; the police and the Special Juvenile Police Unit are informed under POCSO. A woman doctor examines her with the nurse assisting and collecting samples in the evidence kit; the counsellor and social worker support the girl and her mother; the Child Welfare Committee arranges protection; samples go to the forensic laboratory; and the nurse later gives evidence in the Special Court about what she observed and handed over.

Conclusion The forensic team includes the forensic nurse, treating doctors, forensic medicine experts and pathologists, police and crime-scene investigators, forensic scientists and specialists, psychiatrists and psychologists, social workers and counsellors, child protection officials, legal professionals and hospital records staff, each with defined roles. The nurse is the link among them – caring for the victim and assisting in examinations, procedures, specimen handling, consultations and legal formalities that are beyond her own scope, while staying within her competence.

subject: Introduction to Forensic Nursing and Indian Laws
unit_title: Forensic Team and Role of the Forensic Nurse
question: Describe the comprehensive forensic nursing care of the victim and family – physical, psychosocial, cultural and spiritual, and legal aspects.
answer_html:
Introduction Victims of violence – assault, sexual violence, domestic violence, child abuse, elder abuse, acid attacks, attempted murder, trafficking – need comprehensive, holistic and trauma-informed care. The forensic nurse cares for the whole person and the family, while protecting legal rights and evidence.

Principles of care

  • Safety first – medical stability and protection from further harm.
  • Trauma-informed, survivor-centred care – respect, choice, control, avoiding re-traumatisation.
  • Non-judgemental attitude, privacy, dignity and confidentiality.
  • Informed consent for every step.
  • Integration of care with evidence preservation.

1. Physical care

  • Initial assessment – airway, breathing, circulation, level of consciousness; life-threatening injuries treated first.
  • Head-to-toe assessment – injuries (abrasions, bruises, lacerations, burns, fractures, bite marks, strangulation marks), pain, bleeding, signs of poisoning or drugs.
  • Treatment – wound care, splinting, analgesia, fluids, surgery as needed; tetanus prophylaxis; hepatitis B vaccination.
  • In sexual violence – emergency contraception, STI prophylaxis, HIV post-exposure prophylaxis, pregnancy testing.
  • Preserve evidence while treating – cut clothes away from stab or bullet holes, keep clothing in separate paper bags, avoid unnecessary washing before examination (where safe), collect samples before medications when possible (e.g. toxicology).
  • Rest, nutrition, hygiene (once evidence is collected), sleep and comfort.

2. Psychosocial care

  • Psychological first aid – listen, believe, reassure ("You are safe here; it is not your fault"), do not pressurise for details.
  • Crisis intervention – reduce anxiety, help regain control, involve trusted persons.
  • Assess emotional state and risk – fear, shock, numbness, anger, guilt, flashbacks, suicidal thoughts; refer for counselling and psychiatric care.
  • Safety planning – especially in domestic violence (safe place, emergency contacts, documents, helplines 181/112/1098).
  • Support for children – child-friendly environment, presence of a trusted adult, play, age-appropriate explanations.
  • Social support – link with social workers, One Stop Centres, shelters, legal aid, Child Welfare Committee, schemes and victim compensation (BNSS Section 396).

3. Cultural and spiritual care

  • Respect cultural beliefs, gender norms, language and religion; provide interpreters; offer a same-gender caregiver when possible.
  • Be sensitive to stigma, family "honour" and community reactions that may stop victims from seeking help.
  • Allow spiritual practices and visits by religious leaders if desired; support the search for meaning and hope.
  • Respect cultural rites in death and bereavement while following legal requirements.

4. Legal aspects of care

  • Medico-legal registration – recording the case in the MLC register and informing police as required.
  • Free treatment – victims of rape, acid attack and sexual offences against children must receive free immediate treatment in all hospitals (BNSS Section 397).
  • Consent – for examination, evidence collection, photographs and release of information.
  • Mandatory reporting of child sexual abuse (POCSO Section 19); reporting duties for other offences as per law.
  • Documentation – detailed, objective, contemporaneous records of history (in the patient's words), injuries (with body diagrams, measurements and photographs with consent), care given and evidence collected.
  • Evidence collection and chain of custody – correct packaging, labelling, sealing and handover.
  • Confidentiality – no disclosure of identity of sexual offence survivors; records released only to authorised persons.
  • Fitness for statement – informing police or magistrate when the patient can give a statement; dying declaration if needed.
  • Being a witness – the nurse may be summoned to court on the basis of her records.

5. Care of the family

  • Inform and involve the family as the victim wishes; provide privacy for family meetings.
  • Support family members who may be shocked, angry or blaming the victim; educate them on how to support the victim.
  • Assess the safety of other family members, especially children, in domestic violence and child abuse cases.
  • Grief support if the victim dies; explain legal procedures (inquest, post-mortem) sensitively.

6. Discharge planning, referral and follow-up

  • Safe discharge destination; follow-up appointments (wound care, PEP, vaccines, pregnancy and mental health review).
  • Referral to counselling, legal aid, shelters, rehabilitation and vocational support.
  • Coordination with community health workers for continued support.

Nursing diagnoses commonly identified – acute pain related to injuries; risk for infection; fear and anxiety related to the traumatic event; rape-trauma syndrome; risk for suicide or self-harm; disturbed sleep pattern; social isolation related to stigma; and ineffective family coping.

Conclusion Comprehensive forensic nursing care combines physical care (stabilisation, treatment of injuries, prophylaxis, comfort, while preserving evidence), psychosocial care (psychological first aid, crisis intervention, safety planning, social support), cultural and spiritual care (respect for beliefs and gender, interpreters, spiritual support) and legal care (MLC registration, free treatment, consent, reporting, documentation, chain of custody, confidentiality, statements and testimony), together with support for the family and planned discharge, referral and follow-up.

subject: Introduction to Forensic Nursing and Indian Laws
unit_title: Forensic Team and Role of the Forensic Nurse
question: Explain the preservation of evidence – observation, recognition, collection, preservation and documentation of biological and other evidence – and the forwarding of biological samples for forensic examination.

diagram.caption: Steps of evidence handling
labels: observe and recognise – protect from contamination – collect with gloves using proper technique – air-dry and package separately in paper envelopes or containers – label and seal – document in records and chain-of-custody form – store securely at proper temperature – hand over to police with forwarding letter for the forensic science laboratory

answer_html:
Introduction

  • Evidence is anything that helps to prove or disprove a fact in a legal case.
  • In hospitals, nurses often handle evidence first – on the victim's body and clothing, or in samples taken during treatment.
  • Improper handling can destroy evidence or make it legally useless. Careful preservation is therefore a key forensic nursing responsibility.

Types of evidence

  • Biological – blood, semen, saliva, urine, vomitus, gastric contents, hair, skin cells, tissues, nail scrapings.
  • Trace – fibres, soil, glass, paint, gunshot residue.
  • Physical objects – clothing, bullets, pellets, knives, ligatures, foreign bodies, drug containers, suicide notes.
  • Documentary and digital – medical records, photographs, X-rays, CCTV, mobile phones.
  • Testimonial – statements of the patient and witnesses.

1. Observation and recognition

  • Be alert to forensic cases – unexplained injuries, assault, sexual violence, poisoning, burns, gunshot and stab wounds, suspicious deaths, child or elder abuse.
  • Observe and note the patient's general condition, behaviour and statements (record exact words in quotation marks).
  • Recognise evidence on the body – injuries (type, size, shape, colour, location), bite marks, ligature marks, stains, foreign material, odour of alcohol or poison.
  • Recognise evidence on clothing and belongings – tears, cuts, holes, stains, missing buttons.
  • Note who brought the patient, time of arrival and history given.

2. Collection General principles

  • Collect evidence as early as possible, with consent, without delaying life-saving care.
  • Wear gloves and change them between items to prevent cross-contamination.

  • Handle evidence as little as possible; never wash, wipe or alter it unnecessarily. Specific measures

  • Clothing

    • Have the patient undress over a clean sheet or paper.
    • Do not cut through holes, tears or stains – cut along seams.
    • Place each item separately in a paper bag (not plastic – moisture causes decay).
  • Wet stains – air-dry before packaging; or swab with sterile moistened swabs and dry them.
  • Swabs – from bite marks, genital, anal and oral areas in sexual assault (as per kit protocol); air-dried.
  • Nail scrapings and clippings, hair combings and reference hair samples.
  • Bullets, pellets and foreign bodies – remove with gloved fingers or rubber-tipped forceps (metal instruments scratch markings); wrap in gauze and place in a container.
  • Blood and urine – for alcohol, drugs and toxicology, before medications if possible; blood for DNA.
  • Gastric lavage in poisoning – preserve the first sample of gastric contents and vomitus; keep containers of suspected poison.
  • Ligatures (in hanging) – cut away from the knot and preserve the knot intact.

3. Preservation and packaging

  • Package each item separately; seal containers; use leak-proof containers for fluids.
  • Label each package – patient's name and hospital number, MLC number, type of specimen, site, date and time of collection, name and signature of the collector.
  • Seal with hospital seal/tape and sign across the seal.
  • Store securely – a locked cupboard or refrigerator (2–8 °C) for biological samples; avoid heat and sunlight.
  • Preservatives as advised – e.g. saturated common-salt solution for viscera, sodium fluoride for blood alcohol and some poisons, rectified spirit for viscera except in suspected alcohol or phenol poisoning, and formalin only for histopathology (not for toxicology).

4. Documentation

  • Contemporaneous, objective, legible records – time and date of each action; who collected each item; items handed over.
  • Injury documentation – type, size (measured), shape, colour, location relative to anatomical landmarks, on body diagrams; photographs with a scale, with consent.
  • Record exact statements of the patient; avoid opinions ("the patient was assaulted by her husband" is replaced with "patient states, 'My husband hit me with a stick'").
  • Chain-of-custody form – listing each person who handled the evidence, with dates, times and signatures.
  • Do not alter records; corrections with a single line, dated and signed.

5. Forwarding biological samples for forensic examination

  • Samples are forwarded to the forensic science laboratory (FSL) through the police, on the basis of a police requisition, or as per the hospital's medico-legal procedure.
  • Steps:
    1. Prepare a forwarding letter / requisition form listing each sample, the case details (MLC number, FIR number if available), the nature of analysis requested and brief history.
    2. Ensure correct packaging, labelling and sealing; attach a specimen seal impression on the letter for comparison.
    3. Hand over the sealed samples to the investigating officer or authorised police constable against a signed receipt; record in the register and chain-of-custody form.
    4. Maintain the cold chain for samples requiring refrigeration (blood, viscera); dispatch without delay.
    5. Keep copies of all documents in the patient's file.

Common errors to avoid – plastic bags for wet items, combining items in one bag, unlabelled or unsealed samples, washing the patient before evidence collection when it could have waited, losing bullets or clothing, undocumented transfers, and opinions in records.

Conclusion Evidence preservation involves observing and recognising forensic cases and evidence; collecting biological, trace and physical evidence with gloves and proper technique; packaging items separately in paper or suitable containers, labelling, sealing and storing them correctly with appropriate preservatives; documenting injuries, statements and every transfer in a chain-of-custody record; and forwarding sealed biological samples to the forensic science laboratory through the police with proper forms and receipts. Careful handling by the nurse can make the difference between justice and an unresolved case.

subject: Introduction to Forensic Nursing and Indian Laws
unit_title: Forensic Team and Role of the Forensic Nurse
question: Explain the role of the nurse as a witness in a court of law.
answer_html:
Introduction Nurses may be called to court to give evidence in criminal cases (assault, rape, murder, poisoning), civil cases (negligence, compensation) and other proceedings, because they observed the patient, gave care, collected evidence or documented events.

Types of witness

  • Witness of fact (common witness) – states what he or she personally saw, heard or did (e.g. the patient's condition on arrival, statements made, evidence handed over); cannot give opinions.
  • Expert witness – a person with special knowledge, skill or experience who gives an opinion to help the court (e.g. a forensic nurse specialist on standards of care or injury patterns). Expert opinion is relevant under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (Section 39, formerly Section 45 of the Indian Evidence Act).

Summons

  • A summons (subpoena) is a written order of the court to appear on a stated date and time, sometimes with documents. It must be obeyed; failure without good reason may lead to a warrant or penalty. Witnesses may be allowed to appear by video conferencing as permitted under the new laws.

Preparation

  • Inform the hospital authority; obtain and review the relevant records (with permission) to refresh memory.
  • Understand the facts of your involvement; do not discuss the case with parties or the media.
  • Dress neatly and professionally; reach the court on time; carry the summons and identity card.

Stages of giving evidence

  1. Oath or affirmation – to speak the truth.
  2. Examination-in-chief – questions by the lawyer who called the witness (often the public prosecutor).
  3. Cross-examination – questions by the opposing lawyer to test accuracy and credibility.
  4. Re-examination – clarification by the first lawyer on matters raised in cross-examination. The judge may also ask questions.

Conduct in court – guidelines

  • Speak the truth; be calm, polite and confident.
  • Listen carefully to each question; take time; ask for repetition if unclear.
  • Answer only what is asked, briefly and clearly, in simple language; explain technical terms.
  • State facts, not opinions (unless an expert); say "I do not know" or "I do not remember" when appropriate rather than guessing.
  • Refer to records with the court's permission; do not alter or add to records.
  • Do not get angry or argue during cross-examination; address the judge respectfully.
  • Remain until formally released.

Importance of documentation – the nurse's records are often the main evidence; accurate, contemporaneous, objective and complete documentation protects the patient, the nurse and the institution ("if it is not documented, it was not done").

Conclusion A nurse may appear in court as a witness of fact or, when qualified, as an expert witness; after obeying the summons and preparing by reviewing records, she gives evidence on oath through examination-in-chief, cross-examination and re-examination, speaking truthfully, clearly and only about facts within her knowledge, supported by good documentation.

subject: Introduction to Forensic Nursing and Indian Laws
unit_title: Forensic Team and Role of the Forensic Nurse
question: Explain the nurse's responsibilities in the admission, discharge, referral and death of a victim in a medico-legal case.
answer_html:
1. Admission

  • Give immediate emergency care without waiting for police formalities.
  • Inform the medical officer, who registers the case in the MLC register with an MLC number; ensure intimation to the police as per hospital protocol.
  • Record identification – name, age, sex, address, identification marks; for unknown patients, a detailed description and photograph; who brought the patient and when.
  • History in the patient's own words, time and circumstances of the incident.
  • Consent for examination and treatment (or document emergency treatment in the patient's interest).
  • Preserve evidence – clothing, belongings, samples; make an inventory of valuables and hand them over against signature.
  • Place the patient in an appropriate area; ensure security (police guard if required) and privacy.

2. Discharge

  • Ensure that the police are informed before discharge of a medico-legal case, as per hospital policy; the investigating officer may need to record a statement or collect the discharge or injury certificate.
  • Prepare a discharge summary with diagnosis, treatment, condition at discharge and follow-up advice; give copies of medico-legal documents only to authorised persons.
  • If the patient leaves against medical advice (LAMA) or absconds – document carefully (time, circumstances, informed consequences, signatures) and inform the police and authorities.
  • Ensure a safe place for discharge (shelter, One Stop Centre, child welfare committee for children) when the patient may be at risk.

3. Referral and transfer

  • Stabilise the patient; give first aid and treatment.
  • Prepare a referral note with the MLC number, findings, treatment given and reason for referral.
  • Send copies of records; preserved evidence is handed to the police (not sent with the patient unless directed) with chain-of-custody documentation.
  • Inform the receiving hospital and the police; arrange a trained escort and ambulance.

4. Death of the victim

  • Do not remove tubes, catheters, cannulas or dressings unless instructed; do not wash the body or remove clothing that may carry evidence.
  • Inform the medical officer, who declares death and records the time; inform the police immediately.
  • The body is not handed over to relatives in medico-legal cases until the inquest and post-mortem are completed.
  • The police conduct an inquest (under Section 194 of the BNSS; a magistrate's inquest under Section 196 in deaths in custody, dowry deaths within seven years of marriage and similar cases).
  • Prepare the body with identification tags, keep personal belongings safely, and transfer it to the mortuary with documents.
  • Support the family – explain procedures gently, provide privacy for grief, allow religious practices where they do not interfere with evidence.
  • Document all events, times and persons informed.

Conclusion In medico-legal cases, the nurse ensures immediate care, MLC registration, police intimation, identification, history, consent, preservation of evidence and security on admission; informs police and documents carefully at discharge or LAMA; prepares referral notes and handovers during transfer; and, at death, preserves the body and evidence, informs police, awaits inquest and post-mortem, and supports the family, documenting every step.

subject: Introduction to Forensic Nursing and Indian Laws
unit_title: Forensic Team and Role of the Forensic Nurse
question: Explain the recognition and documentation of injuries in forensic cases.
answer_html:
Introduction Correct recognition and documentation of injuries helps in treatment, determining how the injury was caused and supporting legal proceedings. The nurse describes injuries objectively; opinions on the weapon or cause are given by the medical expert.

Types of mechanical injuries

  1. Abrasion – destruction of the superficial layer of skin (epidermis) by friction or pressure (a "graze" or scratch). Pressure abrasions may show the pattern of the object (e.g. tyre marks, ligature marks).
  2. Contusion (bruise) – bleeding into tissues from ruptured small blood vessels caused by blunt force, with intact skin; colour changes over days (red/purple to blue, green, yellow), but estimating age by colour is unreliable and should be left to experts.
  3. Laceration – a tear in the skin caused by blunt force, with irregular, bruised margins, tissue bridges and hair bulbs crushed in the wound.
  4. Incised wound (cut) – caused by a sharp-edged weapon drawn across the skin; clean-cut, regular margins, length greater than depth, bleeds freely.
  5. Stab (punctured) wound – caused by a pointed weapon thrust into the body; depth greater than length; may injure internal organs.
  6. Chop wound – caused by a heavy sharp weapon (axe, sickle) – combination of incision and crushing.
  7. Firearm injuries – entry wound (usually smaller, with abrasion collar, possible soot or tattooing at close range) and exit wound (usually larger, irregular, everted).
  8. Defence wounds – cuts or bruises on the hands and forearms from trying to protect oneself.
  9. Other – burns and scalds, acid injuries, bite marks, ligature and strangulation marks, fractures.

Documentation of injuries

  • Number each injury and describe:
    • type (as observed);
    • size – length × width × depth (measured with a scale, not estimated);
    • shape, colour and margins;
    • exact location in relation to fixed anatomical landmarks (e.g. "5 cm above the right elbow on the outer aspect");
    • direction, presence of foreign material, bleeding, swelling and tenderness.
  • Use body diagrams (body maps) to mark injuries.
  • Photographs – with consent, with a scale and identification label, overall and close-up views, before cleaning or treatment where possible.
  • Record history and statements in the patient's words, time of injury and time of examination.
  • Note inconsistencies between history and injuries (important in child and elder abuse) without accusation.
  • Record treatment given and evidence collected.
  • Write legibly, sign with name, designation, date and time; never alter entries improperly.

Legal categories – the medical officer classifies injuries as simple or grievous hurt (as defined in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, e.g. fractures, permanent loss of sight or hearing, disfiguration of face, injuries endangering life), which affects the charges.

Conclusion Forensic injuries include abrasions, contusions, lacerations, incised, stab, chop and firearm wounds, defence wounds, burns, bites and ligature marks. Nurses recognise them and document each injury objectively – type, measured size, shape, colour, exact location, body diagrams, photographs with scale and consent, and the patient's own words – leaving interpretation to the medical expert.

question: What is the chain of custody?
answer_html: The chain of custody is the documented, unbroken record of the handling of evidence from the time it is collected until it is presented in court – showing who collected it, when and where, who handled or transferred it, and how it was stored. Elements – description of the item, date and time of collection, name and signature of the collector, the seal, each transfer with names, signatures, dates and times, and the place of storage. Importance – it proves that the evidence is genuine and has not been tampered with, lost or contaminated; a broken chain may make the evidence inadmissible or weak in court. Nurses maintain it by labelling, sealing, recording every handover and storing evidence securely.

subject: Introduction to Forensic Nursing and Indian Laws
