question: Name the preservatives used for forensic samples.
answer_html:
Common preservatives used for forensic samples

  1. Saturated solution of common salt (sodium chloride) – the usual preservative for viscera sent for chemical analysis.
  2. Rectified spirit – for viscera, except in suspected poisoning by alcohol, kerosene, phenol, formalin or acetic acid.
  3. Sodium fluoride (with potassium oxalate) – for blood samples for alcohol and certain poisons; fluoride prevents fermentation and oxalate prevents clotting.
  4. 10% formalin – for tissues for histopathology only (not for toxicology).
  5. No preservative – samples for DNA and some toxicology tests are kept dry or refrigerated as advised. Samples are labelled, sealed, refrigerated where required and sent with a sample of the preservative for comparison.

subject: Introduction to Forensic Nursing and Indian Laws
unit_title: Introduction of Indian Constitution and Human Rights
question: Give an introduction to the Constitution of India – its making, Preamble, salient features and main parts – and explain its relevance to health and nursing.
answer_html:
Making of the Constitution

  • The Constitution of India was framed by the Constituent Assembly (first met in December 1946), with Dr Rajendra Prasad as its President and Dr B. R. Ambedkar as Chairman of the Drafting Committee (often called the "chief architect" of the Constitution).
  • It was adopted on 26 November 1949 (now observed as Constitution Day/Samvidhan Divas) and came into force on 26 January 1950 (Republic Day).
  • It is the supreme law of the land – all laws, governments and institutions derive their authority from it and must conform to it.

The Preamble

  • Declares India to be a sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic ("socialist" and "secular" were added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976).
  • Aims to secure for all citizens:
    • Justice – social, economic and political;
    • Liberty – of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship;
    • Equality – of status and opportunity;
    • Fraternity – assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the nation.

Salient features

  1. Lengthiest written constitution in the world – originally 395 articles in 22 parts and 8 schedules; now with 12 schedules and many amendments.
  2. Federal system with a unitary bias – division of powers between the Union and States, with a strong Centre.
  3. Parliamentary form of government – the President as constitutional head; real executive power with the Council of Ministers responsible to Parliament.
  4. Fundamental Rights (Part III) – enforceable in courts.
  5. Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV) – guidelines for the State, not enforceable in courts but fundamental in governance.
  6. Fundamental Duties (Part IVA, Article 51A) – added in 1976.
  7. Independent and integrated judiciary with judicial review – the Supreme Court and High Courts protect the Constitution and rights.
  8. Single citizenship for the whole country.
  9. Universal adult franchise – every citizen aged 18 years and above can vote.
  10. Secular State – equal respect for all religions.
  11. Flexible and rigid – some parts can be amended by simple majority, others need special majority and state ratification (Article 368).
  12. Emergency provisions, independent bodies (Election Commission, CAG, UPSC), and local self-government (Panchayats and Municipalities – 73rd and 74th Amendments, 1992).

Main parts relevant to students

  • Part III – Fundamental Rights (Articles 12–35)
    • Right to equality (14–18).
    • Right to freedom (19–22) – including Article 21: protection of life and personal liberty.
    • Right against exploitation (23–24) – no trafficking, forced labour or child labour in hazardous work.
    • Right to freedom of religion (25–28).
    • Cultural and educational rights (29–30).
    • Right to constitutional remedies (Article 32) – approaching the Supreme Court through writs such as habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto (High Courts under Article 226).
  • Part IV – Directive Principles (Articles 36–51) – health-related articles:
    • Article 39(e) and (f) – protection of health of workers and children from abuse.
    • Article 41 – public assistance in sickness, old age and disability.
    • Article 42 – just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief.
    • Article 47 – duty of the State to raise the level of nutrition and standard of living and improve public health, and to prohibit intoxicating drinks and harmful drugs.
    • Article 48A – protection of the environment.
  • Part IVA – Fundamental Duties – e.g. to respect the Constitution, promote harmony, renounce practices derogatory to women, protect the environment, develop scientific temper and strive for excellence.
  • Seventh Schedule – division of legislative powers:
    • Union List – e.g. defence, international health regulations, port quarantine.
    • State List – public health and sanitation, hospitals and dispensaries.
    • Concurrent List – e.g. medical education and professions, prevention of infectious diseases, criminal law, social security.

Relevance to health and nursing

  • Article 21 has been interpreted by the Supreme Court to include the right to health and medical care, emergency medical treatment (Parmanand Katara case, 1989), dignity, privacy (Puttaswamy case, 2017), a clean environment and the right to die with dignity (passive euthanasia and advance directives, 2018).
  • Equality and non-discrimination (Articles 14–15) require nurses to give care without discrimination by caste, religion, sex or place of birth.
  • Directive Principles guide health policies and programmes – nutrition, maternity benefits, public health, prohibition of harmful substances.
  • Protection of victims and accused – Articles 20–22 and 39A (free legal aid) shape medico-legal procedures.
  • Federal structure – health is mainly a State subject, while national programmes and laws (e.g. nursing regulation, drugs, criminal laws) are made by Parliament or under the Concurrent List.
  • Nurses, as citizens and professionals, have a duty to uphold constitutional values – dignity, equality, liberty and justice – in their practice.

Conclusion The Constitution of India, adopted on 26 November 1949 and effective from 26 January 1950, is the supreme law that declares India a sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic committed to justice, liberty, equality and fraternity. Its salient features include a lengthy written text, federalism with a strong Centre, parliamentary government, fundamental rights, directive principles, fundamental duties, an independent judiciary, single citizenship and universal franchise. Through Article 21, the directive principles and the division of powers, it shapes health care, nursing practice and the protection of victims and accused persons.

subject: Introduction to Forensic Nursing and Indian Laws
unit_title: Introduction of Indian Constitution and Human Rights
question: Explain the rights of victims and the rights of accused persons in India.
answer_html:
Introduction India's criminal justice system aims to punish the guilty, protect the innocent and support victims. Both victims and accused persons have rights under the Constitution and the criminal laws – the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA), in force from 1 July 2024.

A. Rights of victims

  1. Right to report the crime – an FIR can be lodged at any police station irrespective of jurisdiction (zero FIR) and electronically (e-FIR); a free copy of the FIR is given.
  2. Right to information – victims are to be informed about the progress of the investigation.
  3. Right to dignity and privacy
    • Statements of women victims of sexual offences are recorded by a woman police officer, preferably at the victim's residence or a place of her choice.
    • The identity of victims of sexual offences must not be disclosed (BNS Section 72).
    • Trials of rape cases are held in camera.
  4. Right to free medical treatment – all hospitals, public and private, must give immediate free first aid or treatment to victims of rape, acid attack and sexual offences against children (BNSS Section 397).
  5. Right to medical examination with consent (BNSS Section 184 for rape survivors) and to examination by a woman doctor for girl children (POCSO).
  6. Right to compensation and rehabilitation – under the Victim Compensation Scheme (BNSS Section 396), including interim relief.
  7. Right to legal aid and to be heard – free legal services through Legal Services Authorities; the victim may engage a lawyer to assist the prosecution.
  8. Protection of witnesses and victims from intimidation (witness protection schemes).
  9. Support services – One Stop Centres, helplines, child welfare committees and support persons for child victims.

B. Rights of accused persons

  1. Constitutional protections – Article 20
    • No ex post facto punishment – not punished for an act that was not an offence when done.
    • No double jeopardy – not prosecuted and punished twice for the same offence.
    • Protection against self-incrimination – not compelled to be a witness against oneself.
  2. Article 21 – no deprivation of life or personal liberty except by a just, fair and reasonable procedure established by law; includes the right to a speedy and fair trial, humane treatment and freedom from torture.
  3. Article 22 and the BNSS
    • Right to be informed of the grounds of arrest.
    • Right to have a relative or friend informed of the arrest.
    • Right to consult and be defended by a lawyer of choice.
    • Right to be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours of arrest.
  4. Right to bail in bailable offences and to apply for bail in others.
  5. Right to free legal aid (Article 39A; Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987) if unable to afford a lawyer.
  6. Presumption of innocence until proved guilty; right to know the evidence and to cross-examine witnesses.
  7. Right to medical examination – an arrested person may be medically examined, including to show injuries caused by others (examination of the accused under BNSS provisions); the D. K. Basu guidelines (Supreme Court, 1997) require medical examination of detainees and safeguards against custodial violence.
  8. Right to humane treatment in custody and to health care.

Role of the nurse – provide care to both victims and accused without discrimination; respect privacy, consent and confidentiality; give free treatment to eligible victims; document injuries honestly (including those of accused persons, which may reveal custodial violence); and inform patients about support services.

Conclusion Victims have rights to report crimes (zero FIR, e-FIR), information, dignity, privacy and identity protection, free immediate treatment (BNSS 397), consensual medical examination, compensation (BNSS 396), legal aid, protection and support services; accused persons have rights against ex post facto laws, double jeopardy and self-incrimination, to life and liberty with fair procedure, to know the grounds of arrest, to counsel, to production before a magistrate within 24 hours, to bail, legal aid, presumption of innocence, medical examination and humane treatment. Nurses respect the rights of both.

subject: Introduction to Forensic Nursing and Indian Laws
unit_title: Introduction of Indian Constitution and Human Rights
question: Explain human rights and the Human Rights Commission in India.
answer_html:
Meaning

  • Human rights are the basic rights and freedoms that belong to every person by virtue of being human, regardless of nationality, sex, caste, religion, language or any other status.
  • They are universal, inherent, inalienable (cannot be taken away), indivisible and interdependent.
  • The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 defines them as rights relating to life, liberty, equality and dignity guaranteed by the Constitution or embodied in international covenants and enforceable by Indian courts.

International framework – the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR), adopted by the UN on 10 December 1948 (Human Rights Day), and covenants such as the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, the Convention on the Rights of the Child and CEDAW (on discrimination against women).

Human rights relevant to health care – the right to the highest attainable standard of health, to life, dignity, privacy, information, consent, non-discrimination, freedom from torture and cruel treatment, and protection of vulnerable groups (children, women, the elderly, persons with disabilities and mental illness, prisoners).

National Human Rights Commission (NHRC)

  • Established on 12 October 1993 under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, as an independent statutory body with headquarters in New Delhi.
  • Composition – a Chairperson who has been a Chief Justice of India or a judge of the Supreme Court, members with judicial and human rights experience, and ex-officio members – chairpersons of national commissions such as those for women, Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, minorities, Backward Classes and protection of child rights, and the Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities.
  • Functions
    1. Inquire – on its own (suo motu) or on a complaint – into violations of human rights or negligence by public servants in preventing them.
    2. Intervene in court proceedings involving human rights.
    3. Visit jails, prisons and other institutions (e.g. mental health establishments) to study living conditions and recommend improvements.
    4. Review constitutional and legal safeguards and recommend measures.
    5. Study international treaties; promote research and human rights literacy; encourage NGOs.
  • Powers – the powers of a civil court in inquiries (summoning witnesses, requiring documents); recommending compensation, prosecution or disciplinary action; it receives intimation of custodial deaths.
  • Limitations – recommendations are not binding, and it generally does not inquire into matters more than one year old.

State Human Rights Commissions (SHRCs) – in states (e.g. the Maharashtra State Human Rights Commission) with similar functions for state matters; Human Rights Courts in districts for speedy trial of offences arising from violations.

Role of the nurse

  • Respect patients' human rights – dignity, consent, privacy, confidentiality, non-discrimination.
  • Protect vulnerable patients (children, the elderly, persons with mental illness, prisoners) from abuse and neglect.
  • Document and report signs of torture or custodial violence; refuse participation in cruel or degrading practices.
  • Advocate for patients' rights and access to care.

Conclusion Human rights are universal, inalienable rights to life, liberty, equality and dignity, recognised in the UDHR (1948) and protected in India by the Constitution and the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993. The NHRC (1993), State Human Rights Commissions and Human Rights Courts inquire into violations, visit institutions, review safeguards and promote awareness; nurses protect and advocate for the human rights of all patients.

subject: Introduction to Forensic Nursing and Indian Laws
unit_title: Introduction of Indian Constitution and Human Rights
question: What is the Universal Declaration of Human Rights?
answer_html:
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) is a historic document adopted by the United Nations General Assembly on 10 December 1948, setting out, for the first time, fundamental human rights to be universally protected. Human Rights Day is observed every year on 10 December.

  • It has 30 articles, covering civil and political rights (life, liberty, security, freedom from torture and slavery, equality before law, fair trial, privacy, freedom of thought and expression) and economic, social and cultural rights (work, education, social security, and a standard of living adequate for health and well-being, including medical care – Article 25).
  • It forms the basis of international human rights law and has influenced national constitutions, including India's.

subject: Introduction to Forensic Nursing and Indian Laws
unit_title: Introduction of Indian Constitution and Human Rights
question: What is Article 21 of the Constitution? State its importance in health care.
tags: protection of life and personal liberty
answer_html:
Article 21 states: "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law."

  • It applies to all persons (citizens and non-citizens).
  • The Supreme Court has interpreted "life" broadly to mean a life with dignity, including the right to health and medical care, emergency medical treatment (Parmanand Katara v. Union of India, 1989 – every doctor must give immediate care to save life without waiting for legal formalities), privacy (K. S. Puttaswamy, 2017), a clean environment, livelihood, speedy trial and the right to die with dignity (Common Cause, 2018). Importance in health care – it obliges hospitals and health workers to provide emergency care without delay, respect dignity and privacy, and protect patients' rights.

subject: Introduction to Forensic Nursing and Indian Laws
unit_title: Sources of Laws, Indian Judicial System and Indian Laws
question: Explain the sources of law and law-making powers in India. Describe the Indian judicial system and the procedure in civil and criminal cases.

diagram.caption: Hierarchy of courts in India
labels: Supreme Court at the top – High Courts in states – District and Sessions Courts – below them civil courts (Civil Judge Senior and Junior Division) on one side and criminal courts (Chief Judicial Magistrate
Judicial Magistrate First Class and Second Class) on the other
Lok Adalats and consumer commissions alongside

answer_html:
A. Sources of law

  1. The Constitution – the supreme law; all other laws must conform to it.
  2. Legislation (statutes)
    • Acts passed by Parliament and State Legislatures (e.g. the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, POCSO Act, Mental Healthcare Act, State Nursing Council Acts).
    • Ordinances issued by the President or Governor when the legislature is not in session.
  3. Delegated (subordinate) legislation – rules, regulations, notifications and bye-laws made by the government or statutory bodies under the authority of an Act (e.g. Biomedical Waste Management Rules, INC regulations, POCSO Rules).
  4. Judicial precedents (case law) – decisions of higher courts; the law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on all courts in India (Article 141). Examples – Parmanand Katara (emergency care), Jacob Mathew (medical negligence), Common Cause (living wills).
  5. Customs and usages – long-established practices accepted as law in some matters (e.g. certain personal and local customs).
  6. Personal laws – Hindu, Muslim, Christian and Parsi laws on marriage, inheritance and adoption.
  7. International treaties and conventions – ratified treaties influence laws and judicial interpretation (e.g. CEDAW, the Convention on the Rights of the Child).
  8. Equity, justice and good conscience – applied when no specific law exists.

B. Law-making powers

  • The Seventh Schedule distributes legislative powers:
    • Union List – Parliament alone legislates.
    • State List – State Legislatures legislate (e.g. public health, hospitals).
    • Concurrent List – both can legislate, with central law prevailing in case of conflict (e.g. criminal law, medical professions, infectious diseases).
    • Residuary powers lie with Parliament.
  • Process – a Bill is introduced, debated and passed by both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) or the State Legislature, and becomes an Act after the assent of the President (or Governor); it comes into force on the date notified.

C. The Indian judicial system India has a single integrated judiciary:

  1. Supreme Court of India (New Delhi) – the highest court; the Chief Justice of India and other judges. Original jurisdiction (disputes between Centre and States, enforcement of fundamental rights under Article 32), appellate jurisdiction, advisory jurisdiction; guardian of the Constitution.
  2. High Courts – in states or groups of states (e.g. the Bombay High Court, with a bench at Nagpur); writ jurisdiction (Article 226), appeals from subordinate courts, supervision over them.
  3. Subordinate (district) courts
    • District Judge (civil) and Sessions Judge (criminal) – the principal court of the district; the Sessions Court tries serious offences (murder, rape) and can award any sentence permitted by law (a death sentence requires confirmation by the High Court).
    • Civil courts – Civil Judge (Senior Division) and Civil Judge (Junior Division).
    • Criminal courts of magistrates
      • Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM).
      • Judicial Magistrate of the First Class (JMFC) – tries less serious offences and can award imprisonment up to three years and/or fine as provided under the BNSS; records confessions and statements and grants remand.
      • Judicial Magistrate of the Second Class.
    • Executive magistrates (District Magistrate, Sub-Divisional Magistrate, Tahsildar) – maintenance of law and order, inquests in specified cases.
  4. Special courts and tribunals – POCSO Special Courts, Family Courts, Fast-Track Courts, Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions (district, state, national), Lok Adalats (alternative dispute resolution), administrative tribunals.

D. Procedure in civil cases (disputes between private parties – property, contracts, compensation, medical negligence claims)

  1. Plaint filed by the plaintiff in the appropriate court with court fees.
  2. Summons issued to the defendant.
  3. Written statement filed by the defendant.
  4. Framing of issues by the court.
  5. Evidence – documents and witnesses of both sides, with examination and cross-examination.
  6. Arguments.
  7. Judgment and decree – relief such as damages or an injunction.
  8. Appeal to a higher court; execution of the decree. - The burden of proof is "on the balance of probabilities".

E. Procedure in criminal cases (offences against the State and society)

  1. Information about the offence – an FIR is registered for cognizable offences (police can arrest without warrant, e.g. murder, rape, grievous hurt), including zero FIR and e-FIR; for non-cognizable offences, the police need a magistrate's permission to investigate.
  2. Investigation by police – visiting the scene (with forensic experts for serious offences), collecting evidence, recording statements, medical examination of victim and accused, inquest and post-mortem, sending samples to the FSL.
  3. Arrest with safeguards; production before a magistrate within 24 hours; bail or custody.
  4. Police report (charge sheet) filed before the magistrate, within the time limits set by law.
  5. Cognizance of the offence by the court.
  6. Framing of charges (or discharge if there is no case).
  7. Trial – prosecution evidence (examination-in-chief, cross-examination, re-examination of witnesses, including doctors and nurses), statement of the accused, defence evidence, arguments.
  8. Judgment – acquittal or conviction; sentence.
  9. Appeal and revision to higher courts. - The prosecution must prove guilt "beyond reasonable doubt".

Conclusion Indian law comes from the Constitution, legislation, delegated legislation, judicial precedents (binding under Article 141), customs, personal laws, treaties and equity, with law-making powers divided between Parliament and the States through the Seventh Schedule. The integrated judiciary consists of the Supreme Court, High Courts and subordinate courts (district and sessions courts, civil judges, CJM, JMFC and second-class magistrates), plus special courts and tribunals. Civil cases proceed from plaint to decree and are decided on the balance of probabilities, while criminal cases proceed from FIR and investigation through charge sheet, charges and trial to judgment, requiring proof beyond reasonable doubt.

subject: Introduction to Forensic Nursing and Indian Laws
unit_title: Sources of Laws, Indian Judicial System and Indian Laws
question: Give an overview of the new criminal laws – the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 – with provisions relevant to nurses.

diagram.caption: Old and new criminal laws
labels: Indian Penal Code 1860 → Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (substantive law – offences and punishments); Code of Criminal Procedure 1973 → Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 (procedure – FIR
trial); Indian Evidence Act 1872 → Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 (evidence – including electronic records); all in force from 1 July 2024

answer_html:
Introduction

  • Three new criminal laws, passed by Parliament in December 2023, came into force on 1 July 2024, replacing colonial-era laws:
    • the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) replaced the Indian Penal Code, 1860;
    • the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) replaced the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973;
    • the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA) replaced the Indian Evidence Act, 1872.
  • Their stated aims are justice rather than punishment alone, victim-centred procedures, speedy trials, and greater use of technology and forensic science.

1. Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (substantive criminal law – offences and punishments) Key features

  • Offences against women and children brought together in one chapter, placed at the beginning.
  • New offences – organised crime, terrorism, mob lynching and sexual intercourse by deceitful means (false promise of marriage).
  • Community service introduced as a punishment for some petty offences.

  • Gender-neutral provisions for some offences. Provisions relevant to nurses (with former IPC sections)

  • Section 63–64 – definition and punishment of rape (IPC 375–376); Section 70 – gang rape.

  • Section 72 – punishment for disclosing the identity of a victim of rape and certain sexual offences (IPC 228A).
  • Section 74 – assault or criminal force on a woman with intent to outrage her modesty (IPC 354).
  • Section 80 – dowry death (IPC 304B); Section 85 – cruelty by husband or relatives (IPC 498A).
  • Section 103 – punishment for murder (IPC 302).
  • Section 106(1) – causing death by negligence (IPC 304A): up to five years' imprisonment and fine in general, but if done by a registered medical practitioner while performing a medical procedure, up to two years and fine.
  • Provisions on hurt and grievous hurt, acid attacks, abetment of suicide, causing miscarriage, and offences relating to public health (adulteration, negligent conduct with poisons).
  • General exceptions relevant to health care – acts done in good faith for a person's benefit with consent, or in emergencies without consent, are protected.

2. Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (criminal procedure)

  • Zero FIR and e-FIR – information can be given at any police station or electronically; free copy of FIR to the informant/victim.
  • Mandatory forensic investigation – for offences punishable with seven years or more, a forensic expert must visit the crime scene and evidence collection must be video-recorded (Section 176(3)), as notified by each state.
  • Audio-video recording of statements, searches and seizures; electronic summons; trials and evidence through video conferencing.
  • Medical examination of a rape victim by a registered medical practitioner with her consent, without delay, with the report sent to the investigating officer within a fixed time (Section 184, formerly CrPC 164A).
  • Medical examination of the accused at the request of police (Sections 51–52).
  • Inquest – by police into unnatural deaths (Section 194, formerly CrPC 174) and by a magistrate in custodial and specified deaths (Section 196, formerly CrPC 176).
  • Victim compensation scheme (Section 396, formerly CrPC 357A).
  • Free immediate treatment of victims of rape, acid attack and sexual offences against children by all hospitals, public or private (Section 397, formerly CrPC 357C); failure is punishable under the BNS.
  • Timelines – fixed time limits for investigation of sexual offences, filing of charge sheets, framing of charges and delivering judgments; trials in absentia of proclaimed offenders.

3. Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (law of evidence)

  • Electronic and digital records (emails, messages, CCTV, electronic health records, video recordings) are treated as documents and can be primary evidence, with certification requirements.
  • Section 26 – statements of persons who are dead or cannot be found, including dying declarations (formerly Section 32 of the Indian Evidence Act).
  • Section 39 – opinion of experts (formerly Section 45) – doctors, forensic scientists and qualified forensic nurses as expert witnesses.
  • Rules on oral and documentary evidence, burden of proof, presumptions and examination of witnesses (examination-in-chief, cross-examination, re-examination).

Implications for nurses

  • Provide free, immediate treatment to eligible victims without waiting for police formalities (BNSS 397).
  • Ensure consent, privacy and timely medical examination of rape survivors, assisting the examining doctor (BNSS 184); never disclose the identity of survivors (BNS 72).
  • Preserve evidence and maintain the chain of custody – forensic evidence is now central to investigation.
  • Maintain accurate electronic and paper records, which are admissible evidence (BSA); avoid altering records.
  • Be aware of liability for negligence (BNS 106) – practise within the scope of competence, follow protocols and document care.
  • Inform the police in medico-legal deaths and cooperate with inquests (BNSS 194, 196).
  • Be prepared to give evidence in person or by video conferencing.

Conclusion The BNS (replacing the IPC), BNSS (replacing the CrPC) and BSA (replacing the Indian Evidence Act), in force from 1 July 2024, modernise India's criminal law with victim-centred, technology- and forensic-driven procedures. Provisions most relevant to nurses include those on sexual offences and protection of victims' identity, dowry death and cruelty, murder, death by negligence (lower punishment for registered medical practitioners), zero FIR, mandatory forensic investigation, medical examination of rape survivors, inquests, victim compensation, free treatment of victims, and recognition of electronic records, dying declarations and expert opinion as evidence.

unit_title: Sources of Laws, Indian Judicial System and Indian Laws
question: Explain the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012 and its importance.
answer_html:
Introduction

  • The Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012 is a special, gender-neutral law to protect children (persons below 18 years) from sexual assault, sexual harassment and pornography, and to provide child-friendly procedures for reporting, investigation and trial.
  • It came into force in November 2012 and was strengthened by the 2019 Amendment (enhanced punishments, including the death penalty for aggravated penetrative sexual assault), along with the POCSO Rules, 2020.

Offences

  1. Penetrative sexual assault (Section 3) and aggravated penetrative sexual assault (Section 5 – e.g. by police, public servants, staff of hospitals, institutions or schools, relatives, gang assault, assault on a child below 12 years, causing grievous injury) – punishable with long imprisonment (minimum ten to twenty years, up to life or death in aggravated cases).
  2. Sexual assault (non-penetrative, with sexual intent – touching) and aggravated sexual assault.
  3. Sexual harassment – sexual remarks, gestures, showing pornography, stalking, threatening.
  4. Using a child for pornographic purposes and storing child pornographic material.
  5. Abetment and attempt of these offences are also punishable.

Key provisions

  • Mandatory reporting (Section 19) – any person, including doctors, nurses and teachers, who knows or suspects that an offence has been committed must report it to the Special Juvenile Police Unit (SJPU) or the local police.
  • Failure to report (Section 21) is punishable with imprisonment and/or fine; there is also punishment for false complaints made to harm someone.
  • Recording of the child's statement – at the child's residence or a place of choice, by a woman police officer (not below the rank of sub-inspector) in plain clothes, in the presence of a parent or trusted person; the child is not detained at the police station overnight.
  • Medical examination (Section 27) – in the presence of a parent or trusted person; a girl child must be examined by a woman doctor; examination and emergency medical care are not delayed for want of an FIR or magistrate's order. The Rules require free emergency medical treatment by hospitals.
  • Special Courts – trial in camera, child-friendly atmosphere, the child not exposed to the accused, breaks during testimony, interpreters and special educators; evidence of the child to be recorded within 30 days of cognizance and trial completed, as far as possible, within one year.
  • Presumption – the court presumes the accused guilty of certain offences unless proved otherwise (reversal of burden of proof).
  • Privacy – the identity of the child must not be disclosed by media or anyone.
  • Support persons assigned by the Child Welfare Committee; compensation for medical treatment and rehabilitation.
  • Monitoring by the National and State Commissions for Protection of Child Rights; the NCPCR's POCSO e-Box for online complaints.

Importance

  • A comprehensive, child-specific law covering a wide range of sexual offences, for both boys and girls.
  • Mandatory reporting breaks the silence around child sexual abuse, much of which is committed by known persons.
  • Child-friendly procedures reduce re-traumatisation; time-bound trials and strict punishments act as deterrents.
  • Recognises health professionals' role in detection, care, evidence collection and reporting.

Role of the nurse

  • Recognise signs of child sexual abuse; give immediate, free care with sensitivity.
  • Report to the SJPU/police without delay; inform the medical officer; document carefully.
  • Assist the woman doctor during medical examination; collect and preserve evidence; maintain chain of custody.
  • Protect the child's identity and privacy; support the child and family; refer to the Child Welfare Committee and counselling.
  • Educate children, parents and teachers about body safety and the law.

Conclusion The POCSO Act, 2012 (amended 2019) is a gender-neutral law protecting children below 18 years from penetrative and non-penetrative sexual assault, sexual harassment and pornography, with mandatory reporting (Section 19), punishment for non-reporting, child-friendly statement recording and medical examination (Section 27), Special Courts with time-bound trials and protection of identity. It is crucial because most child sexual abuse is hidden, and nurses play a vital role in its detection, care, evidence preservation and reporting.

subject: Introduction to Forensic Nursing and Indian Laws
unit_title: Sources of Laws, Indian Judicial System and Indian Laws
question: What is a zero FIR?
answer_html:
A First Information Report (FIR) is the written record of information about a cognizable offence given to the police; it sets the criminal law in motion. A zero FIR is an FIR that can be registered at any police station, irrespective of where the offence took place (jurisdiction). It is given the number "zero" and then transferred to the police station having jurisdiction for investigation.

  • The concept was recommended after the Nirbhaya case (2012) and is now formally included in the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, which also allows e-FIR (electronic information, signed within a stated time). Importance – victims, especially of sexual offences and serious crimes, can report immediately without being sent from one police station to another, so that evidence and medical examination are not delayed.

subject: Introduction to Forensic Nursing and Indian Laws
unit_title: Sources of Laws, Indian Judicial System and Indian Laws
question: Differentiate between cognizable and non-cognizable offences.
answer_html:
Cognizable offence

  • An offence in which the police can arrest without a warrant and start investigation without a magistrate's order.
  • An FIR is registered.

  • Usually serious offences – murder, rape, dowry death, kidnapping, grievous hurt, acid attack, theft. Non-cognizable offence

  • An offence in which the police cannot arrest without a warrant and need a magistrate's permission to investigate.

  • The information is entered in a separate register (non-cognizable report) and the complainant is referred to the magistrate.
  • Usually less serious offences – simple hurt, defamation, public nuisance. The classification for each offence is given in the First Schedule of the BNSS, which also states whether it is bailable or non-bailable and which court tries it.

subject: Introduction to Forensic Nursing and Indian Laws
unit_title: Sources of Laws, Indian Judicial System and Indian Laws
question: What is a Judicial Magistrate of the First Class (JMFC)?
answer_html:
A Judicial Magistrate of the First Class (JMFC) is a judicial officer of a subordinate criminal court at the district/taluka level, appointed by the State Government in consultation with the High Court and working under the Chief Judicial Magistrate. Functions and powers

  • Tries criminal cases of less serious offences and can award imprisonment up to three years and/or fine (and community service) as provided under the BNSS.
  • Records confessions and statements (including of victims of sexual offences) and may record dying declarations.
  • Grants or refuses bail and remand (police or judicial custody).
  • Takes cognizance of offences on police reports or complaints; issues summons and warrants.
  • Commits serious cases (e.g. murder, rape) to the Sessions Court for trial. Nurses may meet a JMFC when statements of patients are recorded in hospital or when they are summoned as witnesses.
